# How the docstring rewriter works

2026.10.04 · Mr. Radio, for Rick · companion to the documentation rewrite plan (plan 1 of 2)

This page describes the process that rewrites docstrings and checks that nothing was lost. It names the model behind every call and what the call is for, explains the time estimates, and explains how the judges fit in. The measurements behind it are in the [pilot results page](2026.10.04-pilot-claim-recheck-results.md).

## 1. The short version

1. **A Sonnet writer rewrites; nothing else writes.** The judges never touch the text.
2. **The check has three model steps.** Sonnet lists the claims of the old text. Haiku says whether each claim is still in the new text. Opus settles the ones Haiku is unsure of.
3. **The check raises alarms; a reader decides.** In the pilot 300 alarms held 2 real losses.
4. **The judge was nine tenths of the check's time,** because Haiku was reasoning privately before every answer. With that turned off, a judge call takes 2.9 seconds in place of 31.1.
5. **Fable makes no call in the rewrite.** It writes the test pairs that measure whether the judge can be trusted.

## 2. The process as the pilot ran it

![Flow chart of the rewriter as the pilot ran it, eleven steps from lint to merge, each marked with the model that handles it](data:image/png;base64,)

The pilot ran this over the 78 docstrings of the five `task_store_*.py` modules. Steps 4 to 8 are the claim check, built as `cosa.repo.doc_lint.harness_cli`. Step 10 loops back to step 4 for the docstrings that changed.

## 3. Every model call, who makes it and why

| Step | Model | What the call is for | Calls in the pilot | Seconds per call |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2. Write | Sonnet 5.5, as Claude Code worker seats | Rewrite the docstrings of a group of files in plain English, leaving code alone | 4 worker sessions | 795 seconds of agent time in all |
| 4. Extract, first call | Sonnet 5.5 | List every claim the old docstring makes, each with the exact words that state it. Asked twice for two independent lists | 156 (2 per docstring) | 6.1 mean over both extractor calls |
| 4. Extract, second call | Sonnet 5.5 | Ask again about stretches of old text that no quote covers | 67 | |
| 6. Judge | Haiku 4.5 | For each claim, say whether the new docstring states it: present, absent or uncertain. Three runs per list | 468 (6 per docstring) | 31.1 with thinking on; 2.9 with it off |
| 7. Settle | Opus 5.5 | Decide the claims Haiku marked uncertain | 8 | 2.6 |
| 9. Read | Sonnet 5.5, two reader seats | Sort each alarm: history, judge error, moved, real loss, unsure | 2 sessions | 31 minutes wall for both |
| 10. Restore | Sonnet 5.5, author and reviewer seats | Put a lost claim back; check the sentence against the code | 2 sessions | minutes |

Three more uses of a model sit beside the flow, not in it:

| Where | Model | What for |
|---|---|---|
| Reader test | Haiku 4.5 answers, Sonnet 5.5 grades | 26 questions answered from the old text and from the new, graded blind, 3 runs. Shows whether a reader can still find answers. Old 58 of 78, new 61 of 78 |
| Labelled test pairs | Fable 5.1 | Writes docstring pairs with one known claim removed, to measure the judge. Section 6 |
| Running the work | Opus 5.5, the manager seat | Starts the scripts, spawns the seats, compares their results. Makes no judgement on a claim |

A fourth judge exists and was not used in the pilot: the harness can send claims to Jev, a small TypeSafe model, through `--judge-backend jev`. The [judge comparison page](2026.10.01-claim-judge-comparison-jev-haiku-sonnet.md) has its figures.

All Claude calls run through the Claude Code command-line tool under the Max plan, so no call is billed per token.

## 4. How the judges interact with the rewriting

The judges do not rewrite and do not talk to the writer. They sit after it, and what they produce is a list of alarms.

**What the extractor sees.** Only the old docstring. It returns claims such as "returns None when the board is idle", each with a quote. A script then looks for each quote in the old text and throws away any claim whose quote is not there word for word. This stops the model inventing a claim.

**What the judge sees.** The numbered claims and the new docstring. It never sees the old text. It answers one word per claim. Its instruction says a claim that is only related to a sentence, or stated more weakly, is absent.

**What happens to "uncertain".** Those claims go to Opus. A claim still uncertain after Opus is counted absent. Doubt becomes an alarm, never a pass.

**How runs are combined.** Haiku judges each list three times. A claim is called missing when two of the three runs say absent. The three runs agreed on 92% of claims in the pilot.

**What the alarms are worth.** In the pilot the judge raised 300 alarms. Two readers sorted them:

| The readers' verdict | Claims |
|---|---|
| Judge error: the claim is still stated | 143 |
| History, correctly gone | 121 |
| History or judge error, readers differ | 24 |
| Moved to a neighbouring docstring | 10 |
| Real loss | 2 |

So the judge is a net that catches a lot besides fish. Half of its alarms are wrong. That is the safe direction: its instruction pushes it to say absent when in doubt, and the cost is reader time.

**How a loss gets fixed.** Nothing is automatic. A reader marks a claim as a real loss, an author seat writes the sentence back, a reviewer seat checks it against the code, and the claim check runs again on that docstring. In the first rewrite this loop restored 261 claims. In the restored rewrite it found 2 more.

**What the judge cannot do.** It cannot find a claim the extractor never listed. It compares one docstring with its own rewrite, so a fact that moved to the next docstring reads as missing. And it does not check that a kept claim is true of the code.

## 5. The optimisation: turning the judge's thinking off

The Claude command-line tool lets a model reason privately before it answers. For Haiku 4.5 this is on by default. Nobody chose it for the judge.

| Per judge call | Thinking on | Thinking off |
|---|---|---|
| Output tokens | 3,949 | 265 |
| Of which the visible answer | about 200 | about 200 |
| Seconds | 31.1 | 2.9 |

Measured on 2026-10-04 over all 78 pilot docstrings, with the same claims and the same prompt, one judge run in place of three:

| | Thinking on, three runs | Thinking off, one run |
|---|---|---|
| Judge stage | 242.5 minutes | 7.8 minutes |
| Alarms raised | 300 | 220 |
| Real losses found | 2 of 2 | 2 of 2 |
| False alarms (judge errors) raised | 143 | 47 |
| History claims wrongly called present | not applicable: the readers sorted this run's alarms | 8 of 121 |

The fast judge found both losses and raised a third as many false alarms. Its weakness is the last row: it called 8 claims present that are gone. None of those 8 is a loss, but a real loss would be missed the same way. Two losses is too few to give a miss rate.

This was done in a throwaway rig. In the harness it is a small change to `model_transport.py`: a setting for thinking on each model call, with tests. A capped thinking budget is a middle setting that has not been measured.

## 6. How the judge itself is measured

![Flow chart of how the judge is measured: a seeder script plans a change, Fable writes the changed text, a second seat checks the pair, the claim check runs over the pairs, a script scores misses and false alarms](data:image/png;base64,)

The pilot cannot say how often the judge misses a removed claim, because nobody knows in advance which claims the writer removed. The labelled set answers that. A script picks a real docstring and plans one change: delete this clause, weaken that word, or change nothing. Fable writes the changed text. A second seat checks the pair blind. Then the claim check runs over the pairs, and a script counts how many planned removals it caught.

Rick ruled that Fable writes these pairs and judges nothing. It has made 592 calls of a cap of 1,000. The fast judge of section 5 should be run over this set before the sweep relies on it.

## 7. The faster process the measurements point to

![Flow chart of the faster rewriter: lint and select, script fixes, write once, script checks, extract, judge with thinking off, second opinion, one reader, restore, merge](data:image/png;base64,)

| Change from the pilot | Evidence | State |
|---|---|---|
| Leave docstrings with no lint finding alone | 3,751 of 6,228 production docstrings (60%) have none | measured today |
| Fix capitals by script | 13,217 of 20,452 findings (65%) are capitals | measured; the script is not written |
| Write once, with "history may go, reasons and behaviours stay" in the prompt | the first pass lost reasons; the restore pass put 261 back | not tested as one pass |
| Judge with thinking off, one run | section 5 | measured in a rig; miss rate not measured |
| Judge against the whole file's new text | 10 of 300 alarms were facts that moved next door | not built |
| One extractor list | both real losses were in both lists | weak evidence, two losses |
| 8 docstrings at once | the harness runs one at a time by design | not built; needs a rate check against the Max plan's rolling window |
| One reader with a quote check | the quote check sent back 58 notes whose quote was not in the new text; the two readers agreed on the loss count | done by hand today |

## 8. The time estimates and where they come from

Every figure starts from a measurement on the pilot: 78 docstrings holding 19,448 words of old text. Stage times are read from the timestamps of each model session's transcript, so they count time inside model calls.

| Stage | Pilot, measured | Per 1,000 words of old text | Per docstring |
|---|---|---|---|
| Writer, first pass | 795 seconds | 41 seconds | 10 seconds |
| Extractor | 22.5 minutes | 69 seconds | 17 seconds |
| Judge, thinking on, three runs | 242.5 minutes | 12.5 minutes | 187 seconds |
| Judge, thinking off, one run | 7.8 minutes | 24 seconds | 6 seconds |

The work to be done is the 2,477 production docstrings with a lint finding, which hold 327,135 words. The pilot's docstrings are long (249 words on average against 78 across the code base), so the pilot rate can be scaled two ways. Scaling by words assumes time follows the amount of text. Scaling by docstring count assumes every docstring costs the same. Each call has a fixed start-up of a few seconds, so short docstrings cost more per word than long ones, and the true figure lies between the two.

| | Scaled by words | Scaled by docstring count |
|---|---|---|
| Writer | 3.7 hours | 7.0 hours |
| Extractor | 6.3 hours | 11.9 hours |
| Judge as the pilot ran it | 68 hours | 128 hours |
| Judge with thinking off, one run | 2.2 hours | 4.1 hours |
| **Total as the pilot ran it** | **78 hours** | **147 hours** |
| **Total with the fast judge** | **12 hours** | **23 hours** |
| With the fast judge, 8 docstrings at once | about 1.5 hours | about 3 hours |

The earlier figure of 111 hours was the claim check alone over every production docstring, changed or not, scaled by words.

One train a day covers about a seventh of the work: 1.7 to 3.3 hours of model time one at a time with the fast judge, well under an hour at 8 wide.

**What the estimates leave out:**

- The restore step and the reader's time. In the pilot two readers took 31 minutes for 300 alarms.
- The merge pyramid. Today's unit tier alone took 26 minutes.
- The Max plan's rolling limit, which may cap how wide the check can run.
- Any second writing pass. The pilot needed one; the proposed process assumes the writer's prompt removes the need, which is untested.

**What would firm them up:** run the proposed process over one real package and time each stage. That gives a per-docstring rate on docstrings of ordinary length.
